Introduction The digital revolution has brought about a new e-commerce era through which consumers now shop differently than before (Creazza et al., 2023). The internet functions as the primary shopping platform in modern times because it provides users with better convenience and easier access to products than conventional retail stores (Bravo et al., 2022; Creazza et al., 2023). People can now acquire any product from basic necessities to high-end items through simple online purchases. The fast growth of e-commerce has not led to uniform consumer adoption and continued usage because emerging markets face challenges from their limited technological infrastructure and cultural differences and consumer trust issues (Luo et al., 2023). The development of e-commerce in Saudi Arabia has accelerated through government backing under Vision 2030 which works to transform the economy and build digital capabilities (Al-Mushayt et al., 2022). The country experienced an increase in internet users and better logistics networks and digital payment acceptance which established a positive environment for e- commerce expansion. The rapid growth of e-commerce in Saudi Arabia faces resistance from consumers who doubt the quality of products and payment security and retailer reliability (Hajr et al., 2023). The difference between infrastructure development and consumer behavior patterns demonstrates why researchers need to study psychological and social elements that affect e- commerce usage intentions. Consumer behavior analysis stands as a vital factor for e-commerce success because it requires both technological readiness and consumer trust and confidence and positive attitudes. The four variables of attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy and trust in e-commerce work together to determine how likely a consumer will adopt online shopping. E-commerce attitude represents the complete assessment that consumers make about online shopping which determines their perception of its convenience and usefulness and shopping enjoyment (Wang et al., 2023). Consumers who hold positive attitudes toward online shopping are more likely to adopt it because they find it useful and satisfying. The decisions of important social figures such as family members and friends and peers determine how people view e-commerce through subjective norms (Nasrudin et al., 2024). Social norms and collective values in Saudi Arabian culture make others' opinions and actions a powerful force that influences personal decisions. People tend to adopt online shopping behavior after noticing their social network members buying online or promoting digital shopping. Self-efficacy functions as a vital factor because it shows how well a person can handle online platforms while searching for information and finishing transactions (Bartol et al., 2023). People with strong self-efficacy demonstrate reduced anxiety when using e-commerce systems which leads them to shop online more frequently. Trust in e-commerce functions as a fundamental element which affects both consumer attitudes and their purchasing intentions. When customers trust online retailers to maintain honesty and reliability and protect their personal and financial data they establish security feelings which leads to higher online purchasing behavior (Capistrano et al., 2024). Consumers avoid online shopping even when it offers convenience and simple technology because they lack trust in online retailers. The established relationships between these factors need further investigation in Saudi Arabia because the cultural and economic and technological aspects differ from Western markets where most e-commerce theories were developed. The research investigates how attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy and trust in e-commerce influence Saudi Arabian consumers' willingness to use e-commerce. The study investigates how attitude functions as a mediator between trust and intention to use e-commerce to understand the process through which positive consumer perceptions lead to behavioral intentions. The study provides essential knowledge to the existing e-commerce adoption literature while offering practical recommendations for e-commerce platform developers and marketers and policymakers. The research results enable businesses to develop strategies for building trust and improving self-efficacy and social influence to create positive e- commerce attitudes. 2. Literature Review 2.1 E-commerce Adoption E-commerce has revolutionized retail operations and consumer purchasing patterns throughout the entire world (Loo et al., 2025). The digital shopping revolution has transformed customer behavior because it enables people to find product information and evaluate options before making their buying choices. The decision to shop online depends on three main elements which include psychological aspects and social influences and technological capabilities (Hendricks & Mwapwele, 2024). The development of online shopping in Saudi Arabia requires knowledge about behavioral determinants because the market remains in this emerging economy continues to grow. The adoption of e-commerce requires more than technological advancement because it needs consumers to change their behavior and establish trust with online shopping platforms (Religia et al., 2021). The willingness of consumers to shop online depends heavily on their perceptions and beliefs and their confidence in using e-commerce technologies. The Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA) and Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) serve as fundamental frameworks to explain how people form their behavioral intentions. The three factors of attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control which reflects self-efficacy determine how people intend to behave according to these theories. The digital shopping environment requires trust as a fundamental element because it contains built-in security risks that affect product genuineness and payment systems and customer information protection. The research investigates how attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy and trust in e-commerce platforms affect consumer intentions to use e-commerce services. The research investigates how attitude functions as a mediator between trust and intention to understand the complete set of behavioral factors that influence Saudi Arabian e-commerce adoption. 2.2 Attitude toward E-commerce The way people feel about performing specific behaviors determines their overall positive or negative assessment of e- commerce shopping. Behavioral science research shows that attitude stands as a leading indicator for predicting intention (Nasar et al., 2019). Consumers who find online shopping to be convenient and efficient and enjoyable will develop positive attitudes toward it. The combination of uncertainty and poor service and fraud concerns in e-commerce leads to negative attitudes that decrease customer willingness to use these platforms (Ahamed et al., 2015). The digital marketplace determines customer attitudes through their assessment of platform usefulness and user-friendliness and enjoyment and trustworthiness (Li & Wang, 2023). A consumer who experiences smooth transactions, timely deliveries, A. A. Alsadoun et al. /Journal of Project Management 11 (2026) 113 and accurate product descriptions is likely to hold a more positive attitude toward e-commerce. Research also suggests that attitude not only predicts intention but can act as a mediating mechanism through which other variables (such as trust) influence behavior (Wang et al., 2023). In the Saudi context, attitudes toward e-commerce are shaped by cultural, social, and technological elements. As a society transitioning rapidly toward digitalization under Vision 2030, consumers are becoming more open to technology adoption. However, certain segments of the population, particularly older consumers or those less familiar with online systems, may still exhibit cautious attitudes. Hence, the following hypothesis is proposed. H1: Attitude influences intention to use e-commerce. 2.3 Subjective Norms and E-commerce Intention Subjective norms refer to the perceived social pressure to perform or not perform a behavior. They reflect how much an individual believes that important others—such as family, friends, or peers—think they should engage in a particular activity (Nasrudin et al., 2024). In societies characterized by strong social interdependence and collective values, such as Saudi Arabia, subjective norms play a crucial role in shaping behavioral intentions. When influential people in an individual’s life approve of online shopping, that person is more likely to view e-commerce positively and eventually engage in it (Suandewi & Maradona, 2023). This social influence can stem from observing others successfully using online platforms or from recommendations shared within one’s social network. In the digital age, social influence also extends beyond direct relationships—online reviews, influencer marketing, and social media communities create new forms of normative pressure that affect purchase intentions. Subjective norms can operate through both informational influence (providing knowledge or reassurance about the behavior) and normative influence (creating expectations of conformity) (Zhang & Chen, 2023). In emerging markets, where trust in online transactions may still be developing, social approval often acts as a substitute for direct experience—people rely on others’ endorsements to form opinions about online platforms. Therefore, when individuals perceive strong encouragement from their peers or social circles to use e-commerce, they are more likely to form the intention to do so. Hence, the following hypothesis is proposed. H2: Subjective norms influence intention to use e-commerce. 2.4 Self-efficacy and E-commerce Intention Self-efficacy, derived from Bandura’s social cognitive theory, is the belief in one’s ability to perform the actions required to achieve a desired outcome. In the context of e-commerce, self-efficacy reflects a consumer’s confidence in their capability to search for products, evaluate options, make payments, and resolve potential issues during online transactions (Capistrano et al., 2024). Self-efficacy is closely linked to perceived behavioral control, one of the key constructs in the Theory of Planned Behavior. It influences how individuals handle technological interfaces and perceived risks. A person with high e-commerce self-efficacy is more likely to feel in control and less intimidated by the idea of shopping online (Suryawirawan, 2021). In contrast, individuals who doubt their ability to use online platforms efficiently may experience anxiety, leading to avoidance of online shopping. E-commerce self-efficacy can be strengthened through prior experience, user-friendly website design, and clear guidance provided by retailers (Bartol et al., 2023). For instance, easy navigation, responsive customer service, and transparent return policies can enhance users’ confidence and perceived control. Moreover, as digital literacy grows among Saudi consumers, the role of self-efficacy in promoting online shopping becomes even more pronounced. In essence, consumers who believe in their own competence to manage online transactions are more likely to develop strong intentions to purchase through e- commerce channels. Hence, the following hypothesis is proposed. H3: Self-efficacy influences intention to use e-commerce. 2.5 Trust in E-commerce Trust in e-commerce is arguably one of the most critical factors influencing online consumer behavior. Trust reduces the perception of risk, builds confidence in online transactions, and encourages repeat purchases (Capistrano et al., 2024). Since e-commerce involves transactions without physical interaction, consumers must rely on their belief that sellers and platforms will fulfill promises regarding product quality, delivery, and security of personal data (Soleimani, 2022). 114 Trust in e-commerce comprises multiple dimensions: competence (the ability of the platform to deliver as expected), benevolence (the belief that the seller has the consumer’s best interest at heart), and integrity (the perception that the seller is honest and transparent). A consumer who perceives an e-commerce platform as trustworthy will not only feel comfortable sharing sensitive information such as credit card details but also develop a positive emotional connection to the platform (Yusuf et al., 2022). In Saudi Arabia, building trust in online shopping remains a major challenge due to historical reliance on traditional in-person retail and concerns over product authenticity or return processes. However, with the expansion of secure payment systems and government regulation of digital markets, trust levels have been improving. Still, trust is not automatically granted—it must be earned through consistent, transparent, and reliable service. Trust influences both attitude and intention. When consumers trust an online platform, they are likely to view online shopping as safe and beneficial, leading to a more favorable attitude (a cognitive-affective response). Simultaneously, this sense of security directly encourages them to engage in e-commerce, strengthening their behavioral intention. Accordingly, the following hypotheses are proposed: H4: Trust in e-commerce influences attitude. H5: Trust in e-commerce influences intention to use e-commerce. 2.6 Mediating Role of Attitude While trust directly affects intention, research suggests that its impact can also be indirectly channeled through attitude (Deresa et al., 2024). Consumers who perceive online platforms as trustworthy are more likely to develop positive evaluations toward e-commerce overall, which subsequently increases their intention to use it (Pop et al., 2023). In this sense, attitude acts as a psychological bridge linking trust to behavioral intention. This mediating mechanism can be explained through the affect– cognition–behavior hierarchy, which posits that cognitive beliefs (such as trust) shape affective responses (attitude), which then lead to behavioral outcomes (intention). If a consumer trusts that an e-commerce platform will deliver authentic products securely and promptly, they form a positive emotional evaluation of online shopping. This positive attitude then motivates them to make a purchase decision (Ho Nguyen et al., 2022). In societies transitioning toward digital commerce, such as Saudi Arabia, where consumers may initially be skeptical of online systems, the formation of positive attitudes becomes critical for translating trust into actual behavior. Without a favorable attitude, even high trust may not fully convert into intention. Thus, examining the mediating effect of attitude provides a deeper understanding of how trust operates in shaping e-commerce adoption. H6: Attitude mediates the relationship between trust in e-commerce and intention to use e-commerce. Fig. 1. Research Model 3. Methodology The research design for this study used quantitative methods to identify elements that drive consumer adoption of e-commerce. The quantitative research design enabled to measure variable relationships objectively while producing dependable statistical findings. The study used a structured questionnaire to collect data because it provided standardized responses which enabled them to perform complex statistical evaluations. The researchers employed convenience sampling to obtain responses from people who were easily available and willing to take part in the study. The research focused on Saudi Arabian residents and citizens because it studied e-commerce adoption patterns in this particular region. The data collection period spanned from A. A. Alsadoun et al. /Journal of Project Management 11 (2026) 115 June to July 2025 and produced 281 valid responses that enabled structural equation modeling and generated significant statistical findings. The research instrument consisted of separate sections which assessed the essential study variables including attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy, trust in e-commerce and intention to use e-commerce. The study employed validated scale items to assess each construct because these items demonstrated both reliability and content validity. The study used Jadil et al. (2022) for attitude assessment through three items and Taylor and Todd (1995) for subjective norms assessment through three items and Kim and Kim (2005) for self-efficacy assessment through four items and Wongkitrunrueng and Assarunt (2020) for trust in e-commerce assessment through five items and Chen and Dubinsky (2003) and Wu and Huang (2023) for intention to use e-commerce assessment through five items. The study used a five-point Likert scale to measure all items which ran from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The five-point Likert scale enabled participants to show their agreement or disagreement with each statement while providing direct measurements of their e-commerce attitudes and perceptions and purchasing intentions. The study performed structural equation modeling (SEM) on their data through SmartPLS software. 4. Results The study participants' demographic information appears in Table 1 which delivers complete details about the research participants. The study participants showed a small male bias because 58% of participants (n = 163) were male while 42% (n = 118) were female. The study achieves generalizable results for male and female consumers because the participant distribution between genders remains relatively equal. Regarding age, the majority of participants were young to middle-aged adults. Most respondents (40%) were between 25–34 years old, followed closely by those aged 35–44 years (38%). A smaller proportion belonged to the 18–25 age group (11%) and 45–54 age group (12%). This indicates that the sample primarily consisted of individuals in their economically active years, who are more likely to engage in online shopping. In terms of education level, most participants held a bachelor’s degree (63%), while 29% had a master’s degree and 8% had an associate degree. This suggests that the sample was relatively well-educated, which may influence their familiarity with digital technologies and online purchasing behavior. Looking at income level, nearly half of the respondents (49%) reported earning between 2,000–3,999 SAR, while 23% earned 4,000–5,999 SAR. About 17% had an income below 2,000 SAR, and 29% earned 10,000 SAR or above, indicating a mix of lower- and middle-income participants with a notable group of high earners. This diversity in income brackets helps capture a range of purchasing capacities and intentions toward e-commerce use. When examining employment status, the largest group were full-time employees (39%), followed by part-time employees (20%) and unemployed individuals (20%). Additionally, 13% were self-employed, and 7% were students, while none reported being retired. This composition shows that the majority of participants were engaged in some form of employment, which aligns with their income levels and purchasing activity. Finally, the data on average online purchases indicates that most participants (59%) made 1–2 online purchases within the observed period, while 31% made 3–5 purchases. A small segment (10%) reported not making any online purchases. No respondents reported purchasing more than five times. This pattern suggests that although most participants have experience with online shopping, their engagement level remains moderate, implying potential for further growth in e-commerce usage among this group. The study demonstrates that psychological and social elements including attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy and trust determine how consumers behave when shopping online. The research demonstrates that consumer attitudes strongly and positively affect their willingness to use e-commerce platforms. People who find online shopping convenient and enjoyable and beneficial tend to shop online more frequently. People who hold positive attitudes toward digital shopping demonstrate confidence and satisfaction because they find online shopping useful and enjoyable (Li & Wang, 2023). The study demonstrates that subjective norms significantly affect consumer behavior because social influences play a crucial role in their purchasing decisions. People tend to shop online when their social environment including family members, friends and peers actively supports their e-commerce activities (Ariansyah et al., 2021). People become more likely to adopt e- commerce platforms because social recommendations and approval create trust and acceptance among users. The ability to use online platforms effectively determines a person's willingness to shop online because self-efficacy acts as a strong predictor of e-commerce adoption. People who demonstrate proficiency in using online platforms to find information and complete purchases and solve problems become more confident in their digital abilities which leads them to shop online (Bartol et al., 2023). People who demonstrate strong digital competencies tend to explore e-commerce opportunities because they feel confident about their abilities. The development of consumer self-control and digital competence leads to increased online shopping participation (Akour et al., 2022). The research established trust in e-commerce as a fundamental element which affects both consumer attitudes and purchasing intentions. The reliability of e-commerce platforms together with their ability to deliver authentic products and secure payment systems leads consumers to develop more positive attitudes toward online shopping (Soleimani, 2022). The study shows that trust directly affects purchase intentions because it influences both how people perceive things and what actions they take (Yusuf et al., 2022). People choose to shop online because they trust that their information stays protected and the platform maintains its performance commitments. The mediating effect of attitude between trust and intention demonstrates that trust influences positive attitudes which subsequently increase purchase intentions. Trust requires emotional and cognitive evaluations that produce security feelings and confidence and satisfaction to transform into actual actions. The research outcomes generate vital theoretical and practical value for researchers, policymakers and e-commerce practitioners who want to boost consumer adoption of online shopping platforms. The research expands knowledge about e- commerce consumer behavior through its validation of attitude, self-efficacy, trust and subjective norms as essential factors that determine e-commerce platform usage intentions. The research confirms that behavioral intentions result from individual beliefs as well as social and psychological elements. The study reveals that trust functions as a direct factor which affects intention and also works indirectly by creating positive attitudes that drive online purchasing behavior. The dual effect shows that consumer trust functions as a fundamental element which enables positive e-commerce adoption attitudes to develop. Online retailers and e-commerce platforms need to establish trust as their main strategic focus according to the research findings. Businesses should build trust with their customers through secure data handling and clear return policies and genuine product information and fast customer service response times. The addition of verified reviews and certifications on the platform will boost consumer confidence regarding its reliability. E-commerce marketers need to develop positive user experiences that deliver efficient and enjoyable online shopping because attitude strongly influences behavioral intention. Online shopping experiences become more positive when customers encounter easy navigation and personalized recommendations and fast payment processing and quick delivery services. The substantial impact of subjective norms demonstrates that social influence through word-of-mouth and social media plays a crucial role in promoting e-commerce adoption. Businesses should use social media platforms together with influencer partnerships and customer feedback to generate positive social media discussions about online shopping. People become more likely to adopt e-commerce platforms after observing trusted individuals who successfully use these platforms. The substantial impact of self-efficacy demonstrates that improving consumer confidence in digital platform usage will lead to higher e-commerce adoption rates. User education programs combined with simple tutorials and dedicated customer support enable new users to develop independent online shopping abilities. User-friendly platforms with straightforward guidance systems will draw in and maintain users who avoid digital shopping because they lack confidence. The research results demonstrate that policymakers and industry stakeholders must develop a protected digital space that maintains transparency for all users. The development of specific consumer protection laws and fair business standards and security education programs will enhance digital commerce trust among the public. The findings hold special importance for emerging markets because they face ongoing doubts about online transactions which prevent people from adopting digital shopping. 6. Conclusion The research investigated which elements affect e-commerce adoption intentions among consumers within emerging markets through an analysis of attitude, subjective norms, self-efficacy and trust factors. The research shows that all these elements work together to determine how much people want to shop online. The study shows that attitude functions as the primary A. A. Alsadoun et al. /Journal of Project Management 11 (2026) 119 factor which determines purchase intentions because positive e-commerce perceptions about convenience and safety and benefits lead consumers to shop online. The study demonstrates that people are more likely to use e-commerce platforms when their social environment including family and friends and peers supports their online activities. The study demonstrates that self-efficacy functions as a vital element because users who believe they can operate online platforms effectively will choose to shop online. The model shows trust in e-commerce acts as a central element because it directly and indirectly affects both attitude and intention. Trust in reliable and transparent online platforms that deliver quality products leads consumers to develop positive attitudes and stronger intentions for online shopping. The study demonstrates that trust functions as a mediator which creates beneficial perceptions that result in actual behavior. The research demonstrates that e-commerce adoption requires both technological systems and psychological confidence and social validation from users. The successful adoption of e-commerce depends on creating trust and improving digital literacy and developing positive online shopping perceptions to increase consumer engagement with digital platforms. The research offers critical information to businesses and marketers and policymakers who want to boost digital consumer participation and maintain long-term growth of online commerce in developing markets. JSON: Name: ecommerce_intent_sem_saudi Title: Quantitative structural equation modeling analysis of psychological and social determinants of intention to use e-commerce among Saudi consumers Short Hypothesis: Increases in consumers' trust in e-commerce cause increases in intention to use e-commerce, with attitude partially mediating this effect. Related Work: Prior work has applied theory-driven frameworks (TRA/TPB, TAM, and extensions) and multivariate models to explain online purchase intention by combining attitude, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control/self-efficacy, and trust. Approaches differ primarily in variable selection and statistical technique: many studies use covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) for theory confirmation, while others use variance-based PLS-SEM for prediction and formative constructs; machine-learning models have been applied sporadically for predictive performance. Limitations across existing studies include heavy reliance on cross-sectional self-report surveys, convenience sampling, limited attention to mediation mechanisms and model comparison, sparse use of behavioral (transactional) outcomes, small-to-moderate sample sizes that constrain model complexity, and limited validation across emerging-market contexts. Comparative weaknesses are a lack of head-to-head evaluation between CB-SEM and PLS-SEM, insufficient ablation of predictor groups (e.g., trust vs social influence), and few studies that quantify incremental predictive gain over standard regression baselines. Abstract: This study addresses which psychological and social factors determine consumers' intention to use e-commerce in Saudi Arabia using quantitative structural equation modeling. We test a theory-driven model where trust, subjective norms, and self-efficacy predict intention directly, and trust also predicts attitude which mediates part of trust's effect on intention. The main contribution is a rigorous empirical pipeline combining measurement validation, PLS-SEM and CB-SEM model comparison, and ablation analyses to quantify the direct and indirect contributions of trust and attitude to explained variance in intention. We expect to (1) estimate path coefficients and their significance using bootstrap inference, (2) report predictive performance (R2) and model fit indices, and (3) demonstrate the relative explanatory power of trust and self-efficacy versus social influence. The expected outcome is a validated, reproducible evaluation of causal pathways informing intervention targets for policy and platform design in emerging-market e-commerce adoption. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Primary survey-collected dataset: cross-sectional questionnaire for Saudi residents, target N>=500 (minimum N=281 for replication), items measuring attitude (3), subjective norms (3), self-efficacy (4), trust (5), intention (5), plus demographics; (B, optional) behavioral dataset: anonymized platform transaction logs for consenting respondents with binary purchase event and frequency for 6 months. Baselines: (1) PLS-SEM (primary), (2) covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM), (3) linear regression predicting continuous intention score, (4) logistic regression predicting binary purchase (behavioral dataset), (5) random forest and XGBoost for predictive comparison. Metrics: measurement: Cronbach's alpha, Composite Reliability, AVE, item loadings; discriminant validity: Fornell–Larcker and HTMT; structural: path coefficients (β), bootstrap t-statistics and p-values (5,000 samples), indirect effect size and significance, R2 for endogenous constructs, f2 effect sizes, SRMR, RMSEA, CFI (for CB-SEM), predictive metrics for ML baselines: RMSE (continuous), AUC-ROC, accuracy, precision, recall (binary/behavioral). Experimental setup: preprocess: remove incomplete responses (>20% missing) and impute remaining via multiple imputation; standardize items; include demographic controls (age, gender, education, income); run PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrap resamples; run CB-SEM and compare fit indices; run 10-fold cross-validation for ML models and report mean±SD metrics; perform measurement invariance tests across age and gender groups. Ablation studies: (A) remove attitude mediator and re-estimate trust→intention path; (B) drop trust construct and compare R2 loss; (C) drop subjective norms and drop self-efficacy separately to measure ΔR2 and Δf2; (D) PLS-SEM vs CB-SEM comparison for estimated parameters and predictive R2; (E) compare survey-based intention prediction to behavioral purchase prediction when behavioral data available. Statistical thresholds: significance at α=0.05; report effect sizes and 95% bootstrap CIs. Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-sectional self-report data produce common-method bias and limit causal inference; convenience sampling or low response rates produce selection bias and limit generalizability beyond the sample and Saudi context; sample size may be insufficient for complex SEM with multiple latent variables and moderators; measurement model misspecification (poor item validity) can bias path estimates; multicollinearity among predictors (trust, attitude, self-efficacy, norms) can inflate variances and distort effect attribution; cultural or temporal shifts (post-policy or market changes) may alter constructs' meanings and reduce replicability; linking survey responses to behavioral logs raises privacy, consent, and matching error risks; CB-SEM assumptions (multivariate normality) may be violated; computational demands for bootstrap and cross-validation increase with sample size but remain modest; results may not generalize to other emerging markets with different regulatory or infrastructural conditions.
